---
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:order_interprets}
We say that a definable strict order $R$ on $M$ \emph{interprets} a linear order $(A, <)$ if $\parallel_{R}$ is an equivalence relation on $M$ and
\[(M/\parallel_{R}, R/\parallel_{R}) \approx (A, <).\]
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:almost_linear_antichains}
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item $R$ interprets a linear order if and only if for each $a \in M$ the set $\operatorname{Inc}_R(a)$ is an antichain.
\item $M$ admitting an order that interprets an infinite linear order is called \emph{almost linear} in \cite{KruTanWag13}.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{def:almost_equal}
We say that two binary relations $R$ and $S$ on $M$ are \emph{almost equal} if there is a cofinite subset $C \subseteq M$ such that $R$ and $S$ agree on $C$: that is, $R(a, b) \iff S(a, b)$ for all $a, b \in C$.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
By minimality, $M$ has the unique non-algebraic type $p$ over $M$. Suppose $\bar M \succ M$ is a monster model. Then $R$ and $S$ are almost equal if and only if they agree on $p(\bar M)^2$.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- fact-1: body_md -->
Let $(M, <)$ be minimal.
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item $M$ has an infinite chain if and only if $M$ has finite chains of arbitrary length.
\item \cite[Proposition 1.1]{Tan05} If $M$ has an infinite chain, then $M$ is countable.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end fact-1 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
Let $<$ be a definable strict order on $M$. The \emph{normalization} of $<$ is a definable strict order $<'$ obtained in the following way:
\begin{compactenum}[(i)]
\item If $(M, <)$ is $\mathrm{Type}(\omega)$, rearrange $I_<(M) \cup U_<(M)$ into an antichain and prepend it to $L_<(M)$. Then $L_{<'}(M) = M$.
\item If $(M, <)$ is $\mathrm{Type}(\omega^*)$, rearrange $I_<(M) \cup L_<(M)$ into an antichain and append it to $U_<(M)$. Then $U_{<'}(M) = M$.
\item If $(M, <)$ is $\mathrm{Type}(\omega +\omega^*)$, rearrange $I_<(M)$ into an antichain and prepend it before $L_<(M) \cup U_<(M)$. Then $I_{<'}(M) = \emptyset, L_{<'}(M) = L_{<}(M) \cup I_{<}(M), U_{<'}(M) = U_{<}(M)$.
\item (pro forma) If $(M, <)$ is $\mathrm{Type}(\emptyset)$, let $<'$ be empty.
\end{compactenum}
We will say that an order $<$ is \emph{normalized} if it is its own normalization.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- fact-2: body_md -->
\label{fact:chains_type}
For a minimal $(M, <)$:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item $M$ contains an infinite ascending chain if and only if $M$ is either $\mathrm{Type}(\omega)$ or $\mathrm{Type}(\omega +\omega^*)$.
\item $M$ contains an infinite descending chain if and only if $M$ is either $\mathrm{Type}(\omega^*)$ or $\mathrm{Type}(\omega +\omega^*)$.
\end{enumerate}
Moreover, a normalized $\mathrm{Type}(\omega)$ structure does not contain a chain of (order-theoretic) order type $\omega + 1$, and a normalized $\mathrm{Type}(\omega^*)$ structure does not contain a chain of order type $1 + \omega^*$.
<!-- end fact-2 -->
<!-- fact-3: body_md -->
\label{fact:type_fixed}
Suppose that $R$ and $S$ are definable strict partial orders on $M$ with infinite chains.
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item If $(M, R)$ is $\mathrm{Type}(\omega)$, then $(M, S)$ is either $\mathrm{Type}(\omega)$ or $\mathrm{Type}(\omega^*)$.
\item If $(M, R)$ is $\mathrm{Type}(\omega +\omega^*)$, then $(M, S)$ is $\mathrm{Type}(\omega +\omega^*)$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end fact-3 -->
<!-- question-1: body_md -->
Let $(M,<)$ be a minimal order with infinite chains. Does $M$ interpret an infinite linear order?
<!-- end question-1 -->
<!-- fact-4: body_md -->
Up to interdefinability, there are exactly two infinite minimal linear orders, namely $(\omega, <)$ and $(\omega + \omega^*, <)$.
<!-- end fact-4 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{def:omega_interpreting}
For a definable strict order $R$ on $M$ that interprets $(\omega, <)$ (in the sense of Definition \ref{def:order_interprets}), we write $\operatorname{Lev}_R \colon M \to \omega$ for the quotient map and define $\operatorname{Lev}^{-1}(n)$ to be the \emph{$n$-th level of $M$} (with respect to $R$).
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:limits}
Suppose that $(M, <)$ is a minimal ordered structure with infinite chains that interprets an infinite linear order. Then:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item $M$ interprets $(\omega, <)$ if and only if $(M, <)$ is either $\mathrm{Type}(\omega)$ or $\mathrm{Type}(\omega^*)$.
\item $M$ interprets $(\omega + \omega^*, <)$ if and only if $(M, <)$ is $\mathrm{Type}(\omega +\omega^*)$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Let $R$ be the definable strict order on $M$ that interprets a linear order $(A, <')$. Then $(A, <')$ abstractly embeds into $(M, R)$ and the existence of infinite increasing or decreasing chains in $(A, <')$ determines the type of $(M, R)$ (up to direction of order) by Fact \ref{fact:chains_type}. This type determines (up to direction) the type of $(M, <)$ by Fact \ref{fact:type_fixed}.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:eq_antichain}
If $E$ is a definable equivalence relation on $M$ with infinitely many classes, then all classes are finite and almost all $E$-classes are antichains with respect to $<$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Since $E$ has infinitely many classes, there can be no infinite (hence cofinite) class. Let $\mathrm{Max} := \{a \in M : a \text{ is maximal in } a/E\}$. $\mathrm{Max}$ is definable and infinite, and therefore cofinite. Hence in almost every class there are no $a, b$ with $a < b$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:omega_extends}                      
Suppose that $R$ is a definable strict order on $M$ that interprets $\omega$. Then $R$ extends $<$ on a cofinite subset of $M$. If $<$ is normalized, then for almost all $a \in M$, we have $\operatorname{Up}_<(a) \subseteq \operatorname{Up}_R(a)$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
First suppose that $<$ is normalized. Let
\[D := \{a \in M : \operatorname{Inc}_R(a) \text{ is an antichain with respect to} <\}.\]
By Lemma \ref{lem:eq_antichain} $D$ is cofinite. For any $a \in D$ and $b \in M$, whenever $a < b$ and $ \lnot a R b$, we have $b R a$. Now suppose for a contradiction that $C := \{a \in M : \exists b \in M (a < b \land \lnot a R b)\}$ is infinite. $C$ is definable, hence cofinite. Construct an infinite sequence $a_0 < a_1 < \ldots \in C \cap D$ inductively as follows. Let $a_0 \in C \cap D$ such that $\operatorname{Up}_<(a_0) \subseteq C \cap D$. Having constructed $a_0, \ldots, a_n$, since $a_n \in C \cap D$, we can choose $a_{n+1}$ witnessing $a_n < a_{n+1} \land a_{n+1} R a_n$. Then $a_0 < a_{n+1}$, hence $a_{n+1} \in \operatorname{Up}_<(a_0) \subseteq C \cap D$ as required.

By construction, $a_0, a_1, \ldots$ is an infinite decreasing sequence with respect to $R$. Then $\operatorname{Lev}_R(a_0), \operatorname{Lev}_R(a_1), \ldots$ is an infinite decreasing sequence in $(\omega, <)$, a contradiction.
For arbitrary $<$, apply this argument to its normalization, which agrees with $<$ on a cofinite subset.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:uniqueness} Assume that $R$ is a definable strict order on $M$ that interprets $\omega$. Then up to almost equality $R$ is the largest definable order on $M$ of $\mathrm{Type}(\omega)$. In particular, any two definable strict orders on $M$ that interpret $\omega$ are almost equal.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
This follows directly from Proposition \ref{prop:omega_extends} applied to an arbitrary definable strict order of $\mathrm{Type}(\omega)$ in place of $<$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:maximal_interprets}
Suppose that $R$ is a normalized definable strict order on $M$ of $\mathrm{Type}(\omega)$ with $R = R^+$. Then $R$ interprets $\omega$.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Take any $x \in M$. As $R$ is normalized, $\operatorname{Inc}_R(x)$ is finite. Suppose $y$ is an $R$-maximal element of $\operatorname{Inc}_R(x)$. We show $\operatorname{Up}_R(y) = \operatorname{Up}_R(x)$. Suppose $z \in \operatorname{Up}_R(y)$. Then $z$ and $x$ are $R$-comparable. If $R(z, x)$ then $R(y, x)$, a contradiction, so $z \in \operatorname{Up}_R(x)$. Hence $\operatorname{Up}_R(y) \subseteq \operatorname{Up}_R(x)$. As $R$ agrees with $R^+$, we have $\lnot R^+(x, y)$, i.e. $\operatorname{Up}_R(y)$ is not a proper subset of $\operatorname{Up}_R(x)$. Now suppose that $y$ is not $R$-minimal in $\operatorname{Inc}_R(x)$. Then there is some $y' \in \operatorname{Inc}_R(x)$ with $R(y', y)$. Then $\operatorname{Up}_R(y') \supsetneq \operatorname{Up}_R(y) = \operatorname{Up}_R(x)$, so $R^+(y',x)$, a contradiction. Hence for all $x \in M$ we have that $\operatorname{Inc}_R(x)$ is an $R$-antichain, so the result follows from Remark \ref{rem:almost_linear_antichains}(i).
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:characterization} Let $R$ be a definable strict order of $\mathrm{Type}(\omega)$.
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item If $R$ is normalized, then $R$ interprets $\omega$ if and only if $R = R^+$.
\item If $R$ interprets $\omega$, then its almost equality class is the greatest class among definable $\mathrm{Type}(\omega)$ orders. Conversely, if there is a maximal such class, then it has a representative that interprets $\omega$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Item (1) and the first part of item (2) follow from Propositions \ref{prop:uniqueness} and \ref{prop:maximal_interprets}. For the ``conversely'' part, let $R$ be a normalized element of a maximal class. Then $R$ is almost equal to $R^{+}$. Let $C$ be a cofinite set on which $R$ and $R^{+}$ agree and let $a \in C$ such that $\operatorname{Up}_R(a) \subseteq C$ (e.g. take $a \in \bigcap_{x \notin C} \operatorname{Up}_R(x)$). Let $S$ be the definable strict order that agrees with $R$ on $\operatorname{Up}_R(a)$ with the elements of $M \setminus \operatorname{Up}_R(a)$ forming an antichain prepended before $\operatorname{Up}_R(a)$. Then $S$ is almost equal to $R$, $S$ is normalized, and $S = S^{+}$. The conclusion follows from item (1).
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- fact-5: body_md -->
\label{fact:order_preorder} $M$ interprets $\omega$ if and only if $M$ admits a definable linear preorder with infinite (strict) chains.
<!-- end fact-5 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:preoder_by_maximal} With the notation as above:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item $P^+(x, y)$ if and only if $P(x, y) \lor A_P(x, y).$
\item $<_{P^+}$ extends $<_P$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
(i) ($\Rightarrow$): assume $P^+(x, y)$ and suppose $\lnot P(x, y)$. If $P(y, x)$, then $y <_P x$, so $x \in \operatorname{Up}_{<_P}(y) \subseteq \operatorname{Up}_{<_P}(x)$, a contradiction. So $y \in \operatorname{Inc}_P(x)$. Suppose there is $z \in \operatorname{Inc}_P(x)$ with $y <_P z$. Then $z \in \operatorname{Up}_{<_P}(y) \setminus \operatorname{Up}_{<_P}(x)$, a contradiction. Hence $y$ is $<_P$-maximal in $\operatorname{Inc}_P(x)$.\\
($\Leftarrow$): if $P(x, y)$ then clearly $P^+(x,y)$. If $A_P(x, y)$, take any $z \in \operatorname{Up}_{<_P}(y)$. Since $y$ is $<_P$-maximal in $\operatorname{Inc}_P(x)$, $x$ and $z$ are $P$-comparable. If $P(z, x)$, then $P(y, x)$, contradicting $A_P(x, y)$. Hence $x <_P z$, and so $z \in \operatorname{Up}_{<_P}(x)$.\\
(ii) $A_P$ only adds edges between $P$-incomparable elements, so $x <_P y \Rightarrow x <_{P^+} y$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:preorder_stab} Let $P$ be a definable preorder on $M$ with infinite chains. If $P = P^+$, then $P$ is linear.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Every bicomparability class of a definable preorder with infinite chains is finite: otherwise it would be cofinite and would meet an infinite strict chain in at least two points. By Lemma \ref{lem:preoder_by_maximal}(ii), this also applies to $P^+$.

First we show that $I_{<_P}(M) = \emptyset$. Assume for a contradiction that $I_{<_P}(M) \neq \emptyset$ and take a $<_P$-maximal $b$ in this finite set. Then $\operatorname{Up}_{<_P}(b)$ is finite and disjoint from $I_{<_P}(M)$. For each $x \in \operatorname{Up}_{<_P}(b)$, the set $\operatorname{Inc}_P(x) \subseteq \operatorname{Inc}_{<_P}(x)$ is finite, and $\operatorname{Inc}_P(b)$ is cofinite. Thus
\[C := \operatorname{Inc}_P(b) \setminus \bigcup\{\operatorname{Inc}_P(x) : x \in \operatorname{Up}_{<_P}(b)\}\]
is cofinite. For any $a \in C$, comparability and transitivity force $a <_P x$ for every $x \in \operatorname{Up}_{<_P}(b)$, so $P^+(a,b)$. Excluding the finitely many elements that are ${P^+}$-bicomparable with $b$, these comparisons are strict. Hence $b \in U_{<_{P^+}}(M)$, which contradicts $P=P^+$. Now $\operatorname{Inc}_P(a)$ is finite for every $a \in M$. If it is nonempty, then $A_P(a,b)$ holds for a $<_P$-maximal $b \in \operatorname{Inc}_P(a)$, again contradicting $P=P^+$ by Lemma \ref{lem:preoder_by_maximal}(i).
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:not_minimal}
Suppose $N = (\omega, <, f)$ is a first-order structure with $<$ interpreted as the usual order and $f \colon \omega \to \omega$ a function such that $f(n) \geq n$ for all $n \in \omega$. Then $N$ is minimal if and only if $f(n) - n$ is eventually constant.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Suppose $N$ is minimal but $f(n) - n$ is not eventually constant. For $m \in \omega$ let $A_m := \{n \in \omega : f(n) - n = m\}$. Each $A_m$ is definable in $N$, but not cofinite, hence finite. Therefore $f(n) - n$ diverges to infinity. Let $k \in \omega$. Then there is $n_0 \in \omega$ such that for all $n \geq n_0$ we have $f(n) \geq n + k$. Hence $\operatorname{Im}(f) \cap [0, n_0 + k)$ has at most $n_0$ elements. Since $k$ is arbitrary, $\operatorname{Im}(f)$ is infinite but not cofinite, contradicting minimality. The other direction is clear.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:bounded_chains}
Suppose that $R$ is a definable strict order on $M$ that interprets $\omega$ and $P$ is a definable preorder on $M$ with infinite chains. Then there exists $B \in \mathbb{N}$ dependent only on $M$ and $P$ such that for almost all $a \in M$, any $R$-chain in $\operatorname{Inc}_P(a)$ has at most $B$ elements.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Let $F:=I_{<_P}(M)$, a finite set. Let $Q$ be a definable preorder that agrees with $P$ on $M\setminus F$, with $F$ (if nonempty) forming one bicomparability class placed before $M \setminus F$. Then all sets $\operatorname{Inc}_Q(x)$ are finite, and for $x \notin F$ we have $\operatorname{Inc}_P(x) \subseteq \operatorname{Inc}_Q(x) \cup F$. Define $f \colon \omega \to \omega$ by setting $f(n)$ to be the largest $m \geq n$ such that $n = m$ or there exist $x, y\in M$ with $\operatorname{Lev}_R(x) = n$, $\operatorname{Lev}_R(y) = m$, and $y \in \operatorname{Inc}_Q(x)$. This maximum exists because the levels and the sets $\operatorname{Inc}_Q(x)$ are finite. The structure $(\omega, <, f)$ is interpreted in $M$ and hence minimal. By Lemma \ref{lem:not_minimal}, there are $k, n_0 \in \omega$ such that $f(n) = n + k$ for all $n \geq n_0$.

Put $D := \{y \in M : \operatorname{Lev}_R(y) < n_0\}$. Outside of the finite set $F \cup D \cup \bigcup_{y \in D} \operatorname{Inc}_Q(y)$, every $x$ and every $y \in \operatorname{Inc}_Q(x)$ have levels at least $n_0$. By symmetry of incomparability we also have $|\operatorname{Lev}_R(y) - \operatorname{Lev}_R(x)| \leq k$. Hence any $R$-chain in $\operatorname{Inc}_Q(x)$ has at most $2k + 1$ elements, and $B := 2k + 1 + |F|$ works for $\operatorname{Inc}_P(x)$. Any two definable strict orders interpreting $\omega$ are almost equal, so their sufficiently high levels agree up to a constant difference. Since every $\operatorname{Inc}_Q(x)$ is finite, the obtained value of $k$ does not depend on this difference. Hence $B$ does not depend on the choice of $R$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:characterization2}
Suppose $P = P_0$ has infinite chains. The following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item $P_{i+1} = P_i$ for some $i \in \omega$.
\item $M$ interprets $\omega$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
(i) $\Rightarrow$ (ii) follows from Lemma \ref{lem:preorder_stab} and Fact \ref{fact:order_preorder}. For (ii) $\Rightarrow$ (i), let $R$ be a definable strict order on $M$ that interprets $\omega$. Let $I_i:=I_{<_{P_i}}(M)$. Since $<_{P_{i+1}}$ extends $<_{P_{i}}$, we have $I_{i+1}\subseteq I_i$. The argument in the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:preorder_stab} shows that if $I_i$ is nonempty, then any $<_{P_i}$-maximal element of $I_i$ belongs to $U_{<_{P_{i+1}}}(M)$. Hence after at most $t = |I_0|$ steps we get $I_t=\emptyset$. So for all $x \in M$ and $i \geq t$, the sets $\operatorname{Inc}_{P_i}(x)$ are all finite.

By Fact \ref{fact:type_fixed}, either all the orders $<_{P_i}$ are of $\mathrm{Type}(\omega)$, or all of them are of $\mathrm{Type}(\omega^*)$.\\
\emph{Case 1: } All orders $<_{P_i}$ are of $\mathrm{Type}(\omega)$. For any $S = P_i$ with $i \geq t$, by Proposition \ref{prop:omega_extends} there exists a cofinite $C \subseteq M$ on which $R$ extends $<_S$. After removing the finite set $\bigcup_{z \notin C} \operatorname{Inc}_S(z)$ from $C$, we can find a cofinite $C' \subseteq C$ such that $\operatorname{Inc}_S(x)\subseteq C$ for every $x \in C'$. If $\operatorname{Inc}_S(x)$ is nonempty, each of its $R$-maximal elements is $<_S$-maximal, and becomes $S^+$-comparable with $x$ by Lemma \ref{lem:preoder_by_maximal}(i). Hence every $R$-chain in $\operatorname{Inc}_{S^+}(x)$ is strictly shorter than the longest $R$-chain in $\operatorname{Inc}_{S}(x)$. By Proposition \ref{prop:bounded_chains}, there is $B \in \mathbb{N}$ bounding the lengths of $R$-chains in $\operatorname{Inc}_{P_t}(x)$ for almost all $x$. Hence we get $\operatorname{Inc}_{P_{t+B}}(x) = \emptyset$ for almost all $x$. All remaining pairs of incomparable elements belong to some finite $F \times F$, so subsequent iterations can only add finitely more pairs, and the sequence stabilizes.\\
\emph{Case 2}: All orders $<_{P_i}$ are of $\mathrm{Type}(\omega^*)$. Repeat the argument for Case 1, replacing $R$ with its reverese (taking a cofinite subset $C \subseteq M$ such that $R$ extends the reverse of $<_S$).
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:order_interprets_order}
If $(M, <, \ldots)$ interprets a linear order by a definable strict order $R$, then $R$ is $<$-definable.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
Suppose $R$ is a definable strict order on $M$ that interprets $\omega$. Then up to almost equality $\parallel_{R}$ is the coarsest definable equivalence relation on $M$ with infinitely many classes.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Directly from Lemma \ref{lem:eq_antichain}: if a definable equivalence relation $E$ has infinitely many classes, then for almost all $a \in M$ we have $a/E \subseteq \operatorname{Inc}_R(a)$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- fact-6: body_md -->
$(\omega, \leq, \operatorname{succ}, 0)$ has quantifier elimination.
<!-- end fact-6 -->
<!-- fact-7: body_md -->
\label{fact:submonoid}
$\leq_H$ is a partial order if and only if $H \subseteq (\mathbb{N}, +)$ is a submonoid.
<!-- end fact-7 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Reflexivity is equivalent to $0 \in H$. For transitivity, $a \leq_H b \land b \leq_H c \Rightarrow a \leq_H c$ is equivalent to $b - a \in H \land c - b \in H \Rightarrow c - a \in H$.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
Let $R$ be an order definable in $(\omega, \leq)$ with infinite increasing chains (so that its strict part is $\mathrm{Type}(\omega)$). Then there is a cofinite submonoid $H \subseteq (\mathbb{N}, +)$ such that $R$ is almost equal to $\leq_H$.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
By quantifier elimination in $(\omega, \leq, \operatorname{succ}, 0)$, $R(x,y)$ eventually depends only on the difference $y-x$. There is no $d > 0$ such that $R(x+d, x)$ holds for cofinitely many $x \in \omega$: otherwise there would exist an infinite descending $R$-chain, contradicting that $R$ is $\mathrm{Type}(\omega)$. Let $H := \{d \in \mathbb{N}: R(x, x+d) \text{ for almost all } x\}$. Then $R$ agrees with $\leq_H$ on a cofinite set. By Fact \ref{fact:submonoid}, $H$ is a submonoid of $(\mathbb{N},+)$. It is clearly cofinite.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:stable_embedding}
Let $\mathbb{M} = (M, <)$ be a minimal structure in a pure order language with $L(M)$ infinite, and consider its substructure $\mathbb{L} = (L(M), <)$. Then for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Any subset of $L(M)^n$ definable in $\mathbb{L}$ is a trace of a subset of $M^n$ definable in $\mathbb{M}$.
\item For any subset $X \subseteq M^n$ definable in $\mathbb{M}$, its trace $X \cap L(M)^n$ is definable in $\mathbb{L}$.
\end{enumerate}
In particular, $\mathbb{L}$ is minimal and stably embedded in $\mathbb{M}$.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:n_to_one}
Let $M$ be an arbitrary structure that interprets an infinite linear order in some dimension $n > 0$. Then $M$ interprets an infinite linear order in dimension $1$. Moreover, if the original interpreted order is $(\omega,<)$, the order interpreted in dimension $1$ can also be chosen to be $(\omega,<)$.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
We proceed by induction on $n$. Suppose $M$ interprets an infinite linear order in dimension $n$ with $n > 1$. Assume without loss of generality that the domain of interpretation is the whole $M^n$. Let $<$ be a definable strict order on $M^n$ such that $E := \parallel_{<}$ is an equivalence relation with infinitely many classes and let $A = (M^n/E, </E)$ be the quotient linear order. For $m \in M$ define
\[C(m) := \{(m, m_2, \ldots, m_n)/E : m_2, \ldots, m_n \in M\}.\]
Then $C(m)$ is a nonempty chain in $A$. If for some $m \in M$ the set $C(m)$ is infinite, we define the relation $R$ on $M^{n-1}$ by $R(\bar m_1, \bar m_2) \iff m \bar m_1 < m \bar m_2$. Then $R$ is an order witnessing that $M$ interprets an infinite linear order in dimension $n-1$.

Otherwise, if for each $m \in M$ the set $C(m)$ is finite, let $<_{\text{colex}}$ be the colexicographical order on $\operatorname{Fin}(A)$, the family of finite subsets of $A$:
\[X <_{\text{colex}} Y \iff X \neq Y \text{ and } \forall x \in X \setminus Y ~ \exists y \in Y \setminus X ~x < y.\]
Then $<_{\text{colex}}$ is a linear order on $\operatorname{Fin}(A)$ and on $B := \{C(m) : m \in M\} \subseteq \operatorname{Fin}(A)$. $B$ is infinite since $\bigcup B = A$. Let $S$ be the pullback of $<_{\text{colex}}$ by the map $M \ni m \mapsto C(m) \in B$. Then $S$ is clearly a definable strict order on $M$ which interprets $B$.
For the ``moreover'' part, every infinite suborder of $\omega$ has order type $\omega$, and $(\operatorname{Fin}(\omega),<_{\text{colex}})$ has order type $\omega$ via $X\mapsto\sum_{k \in X}2^k$. Hence both branches of the induction preserve order type $\omega$.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:interpretation_M_LM}
Let $\mathbb{M} = (M, <, \ldots)$ be a minimal relational structure with $<$ of $\mathrm{Type}(\omega +\omega^*)$ and $\mathbb{L} = (L(M), <, \ldots)$ its substructure. If $\mathbb{L}$ is minimal and interprets an infinite linear order, then $\mathbb{M}$ interprets an infinite linear order.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Let $\mathbb{M}'$ and $\mathbb{L}'$ be reducts of $\mathbb{M}$ and $\mathbb{L}$ respectively to the pure language of orders. Assume that $\mathbb{L}$ interprets an infinite linear order via a definable strict partial order $R$ on $L(M)$. Then $R$ is definable in $\mathbb{L}'$ and by Theorem \ref{thm:stable_embedding}, there exists in $\mathbb{M}'$ an $<$-definable relation $S$ whose trace on $L(M)$ agrees with $R$. Let $\phi(x)$ say ``$S$ restricted to $\operatorname{Low}_<(x)$ is a strict order and $\parallel_{S}$ restricted to $\operatorname{Low}_<(x)$ is an equivalence relation''. Then $\phi(x)$ is a definable property that is true in $\mathbb{M}$ for all $x \in L(M)$. By minimality, there is some $a \in U(M)$ so that $\mathbb{M} \models \phi(a)$. Since $\operatorname{Low}_<(a)$ is cofinite, the conclusion follows.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:question_variants}
The following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item Every minimal ordered structure with infinite chains interprets an infinite linear order in some dimension.
\item Every minimal ordered structure with infinite chains interprets an infinite linear order in dimension $1$.
\item Every minimal ordered structure of $\mathrm{Type}(\omega)$ interprets $(\omega, <)$ in some dimension.
\item Every minimal ordered structure of $\mathrm{Type}(\omega)$ interprets $(\omega, <)$ in dimension $1$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Proposition \ref{prop:n_to_one} establishes equivalence between (1) and (2) and between (3) and (4). Item (2) implies (4) using Lemma \ref{lem:limits}. We show (4) $\Rightarrow$ (1). Suppose $\mathbb{M} = (M, <, \ldots)$ is a minimal ordered structure with infinite chains. If $\mathbb{M}$ is not $\mathrm{Type}(\omega +\omega^*)$, item (4) immediately applies (possibly after reversing the order). If $\mathbb{M}$ is of $\mathrm{Type}(\omega +\omega^*)$, pass to the pure-order reducts $\mathbb{M}' = (M, <)$ and $\mathbb{L}' = (L(M), <)$. Then $\mathbb{M}'$ is minimal and, by Theorem \ref{thm:stable_embedding}, so is $\mathbb{L}'$. By assumption $\mathbb{L}'$ interprets $(\omega,<)$, and Proposition \ref{prop:interpretation_M_LM} can be applied: $\mathbb{M}'$ (and therefore $\mathbb{M}$) interprets an infinite linear order.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
